name: 日本橋 玉ゐ 本店
cuisine: Anago specialist in a 1953 wooden house behind the Takashimaya annex — the house dish is 箱めし, a lacquered box of rice under whole wild conger, served 煮上げ (simmered), 焼き上げ (grilled) or 合いのせ (both) at ¥2,500 small / ¥3,800 medium / ¥4,600 large, with a ¥200 pot of stock drawn from the grilled bones to finish it as chazuke; anago kaiseki ¥6,100–¥8,200
neighborhood: Nihonbashi 2-chōme, behind the Takashimaya S.C. annex — 3 min from Nihonbashi Station (Ginza, Tōzai and Toei Asakusa lines), 106 m by Tabelog's measure; 8 min from Tokyo Station's Yaesu exit
gf_detail: Gluten is in the signature dish itself. The house tare 「つめだれ」 — described by the shop's own representative as its lifeline — is 砂糖と醤油, sugar and ordinary wheat soy sauce, and it goes over the eel in every box. Anago tempura and a 天重 are worked in the same kitchen in wheat batter. No gluten-free tamari, no allergen sheet and no wheat-free preparation appears anywhere on anago-tamai.com. There is nothing here a celiac can safely order.
vegan_detail: A single-ingredient conger house: every item on the お品書き is anago, and even the optional finishing stock is boiled from grilled anago bones. Nothing vegan is offered or advertised.

roles: 創業者・代表取締役 (founder / representative director, per the 2022 Chūō ward interview)
元江戸前寿司職人 (former Edomae sushi chef)
chef_bio.origin: Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku — the shop has never left the block it opened on
chef_bio.background: Tamai opened in June 2005 and is unusual in Nihonbashi for being deliberately young: Satō says the aim is to become a 「平成生まれの老舗」, an old establishment born in the Heisei era. He and a group of Edomae sushi chefs started it after a customer at their sushi counter said aloud that Tokyo needed an anago specialist; the shop is named for Tamai-san, a senior sushi colleague who helped found it. The premises came from another regular — the owner of the Kawaguchi sake shop then in the building, who was closing up and offered them the lease, and who still owns it. The building is a wooden Japanese house put up in 1953, just after the war, as that sake shop. The kitchen buys only wild conger, in season, through Toyosu rather than by boat contract, following the run from the Inland Sea in spring to Edomae in early summer, Jōban and Sendai in late summer and Tsushima in winter; the autumn catch is processed fresh and held at minus 60 so the shop can serve consistently year-round. The 箱めし came out of a courtesy to the trade: tempura shops use 120 g eels and sushi counters 150–180 g, so Tamai took the sizes nobody wanted — 70 cm, 300 g fish and the small 「めそ」 — and built a dish around them. Michelin first awarded a Bib Gourmand in 2015. The operating company, 株式会社バレンタインブルーコーポレーション, today lists 松本純男 as 代表取締役, and there are now branches at Muromachi, Coredo Muromachi, LaQua, Ginza, Shin-Yokohama, Narita Airport, Seoul and Taipei.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「平成生まれの老舗」 — build an old shop from scratch. Take the eel sizes the rest of the trade cannot use, buy only wild fish in season, and let sushi-counter knife work do the rest.
chef_bio.specialty: 箱めし — whole wild anago over rice in a lacquered box, simmered, grilled or both, finished as chazuke with stock drawn from the grilled bones.

anecdotes.text: The premises came from a customer: the man who owned the Kawaguchi sake shop in the building overheard the chefs talking about wanting a place, said he was closing up anyway, and offered them the lease. He is still the landlord.

Tempura shops use 120 g conger and sushi counters 150–180 g, so Tamai deliberately buys the 300 g / 70 cm fish and the small 'meso' nobody else wants — the 箱めし exists partly so as not to compete with its neighbours for stock.
The house went up in 1953 as a sake shop and stands behind the Takashimaya S.C. annex; it is easy to walk straight past.
Raw anago sashimi is served only from early July to late September, and only at the Honten, the Muromachi branch and Ginza Tamai.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every dish on the menu is conger eel; even the optional stock is boiled from grilled anago bones.

positives.text: Ordering is simple and visible — three box sizes and a choice of simmered or grilled — and the site runs in English, Korean and Chinese, so it is easy to know exactly what you are being given.

cultural_comfort.note: A wooden house with 25 seats — tables plus a six-seat counter — all non-smoking, cards accepted (VISA/Master/JCB/AMEX/Diners), children welcome. Reservations at the Honten are taken for dinner only, by phone on 03-3272-3227; lunch is walk-in and queues. A ¥400 otōshi is charged in the evening. The website runs in English, Korean and Chinese and the menu is short enough to point at.

name: 銀座 天一 日本橋室町店
address_ja: 〒103-0022 東京都中央区日本橋室町2-4-3 日本橋室町野村ビル YUITO 3F
cuisine: Counter Edomae tempura from the 1930 Ginza house Ten-ichi, on the third floor of the YUITO building — table lunch is the 特製天丼 at ¥4,950, counter courses run ¥6,600 / ¥8,800 / ¥12,100 at lunch and ¥13,200 / ¥16,500 / ¥18,700 (the Muromachi 特選) at dinner
neighborhood: Nihonbashi-Muromachi 2-chōme — directly connected to Mitsukoshimae Station exit A9 (Ginza and Hanzōmon lines, about 1 min); 1–3 min from Shin-Nihonbashi (JR Sōbu), 7–8 min from Nihonbashi Station exits B11/B12
gf_detail: Ten-ichi answers this directly in its own FAQ and the answer is no: 「天ぷら粉の特性上、グルテンフリー対応はできかねます」 — given what tempura flour is, they cannot do gluten-free. The same FAQ goes further and says that for safety they will not accept a reservation at all from a guest with an egg, wheat, soy or sesame allergy, because 「当店ではすべての食材を同一の揚げ油で調理しております」 — every ingredient goes through one shared fryer. That is a shop declining to guarantee, in its own words, and it is the clearest possible 'no' in this tranche.
vegan_detail: The same FAQ states 「ヴィーガン、ベジタリアン、ハラール対応は可能です。事前にお申し付けください」 — vegan, vegetarian and halal courses are available if arranged in advance. Take that as a menu accommodation rather than a clean kitchen: the shop also says every ingredient is cooked in the same oil, so a vegan course here will be vegetable tempura fried in oil that has had prawns and fish through it. Fine for a dietary vegan, not for someone who needs strict separation, and it must be booked ahead.

roles: 創業者 (founder of Ten-ichi, 1930)
chef_bio.origin: Ningyōchō, Tokyo — where the first shop opened in 1930
chef_bio.background: Ten-ichi began in 1930 (Shōwa 5) as a small tempura shop in Ningyōchō and became, in its own telling, one of the houses that turned tempura into counter theatre — food fried in front of the guest rather than carried out from a kitchen. It moved into Ginza Nishi 8-chōme in 1932 and it was there that it became the expensive Ginza tempura house, feeding writers, GHQ officers and, over the decades, a startling roll of visiting heads of state. The company's own history page is not shy about it: Tanizaki Jun'ichirō in 1955, Shiga Naoya in 1957, Mrs Kissinger in 1975, Pelé in 1978, Nixon in 1983, the Gorbachevs in 1995, Clinton with Prime Minister Obuchi in 1998. Ten-ichi describes itself in that period as a 「サロン」 — the Shirakaba-school writers, Bernard Leach and Hamada Shōji among them, met across its counters. The house also has a technical streak: in 1933 it was fitting extractor fans, prototyping German stainless pans and blending corn oil into its frying fat. Founder Yabuki Isao collected calligraphy and painting from the writers who ate there — Mushanokōji Saneatsu, Shiga Naoya, Kishida Ryūsei — and in 1997 that collection opened as the Ten-ichi Museum in Gunma, in a building by the architect Yoshimura Junzō. The Nihonbashi Muromachi branch is a later chapter: it opened in 2010 in the YUITO complex in the Nomura building, positioned as a quieter, business-district room serving what the company calls 「心と五感に響く正統な江戸前天ぷら」. The Ginza flagship was rebuilt in 2022 and a Haneda Terminal 3 branch followed in 2024.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「天ぷらと、一生。」 — a lifetime with tempura. Orthodox Edomae frying, seasonal ingredients, and a counter treated as a room where people talk.
chef_bio.specialty: Counter-fried Edomae tempura courses; at Muromachi the 特製天丼 at lunch and the house 室町特選 course at dinner.

anecdotes.text: In 1933, three years in, the shop was already installing extractor fans, testing German stainless-steel pans and blending corn oil into its frying fat — technical fiddling is part of the house identity.
In 1985 Ten-ichi opened 天一山 above the flagship: one party per day, and over the years the UN Secretary-General Pérez de Cuéllar and President Chirac ate there.
The founder's collection of calligraphy and paintings from the writers who ate at his counter became the Ten-ichi Museum in Gunma in 1997, in a building designed by Yoshimura Junzō.
The Muromachi branch opened in 2010 in the YUITO complex and connects straight to Mitsukoshimae exit A9 — you can reach the counter without going outside.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tenichi.co.jp is a full corporate site. The branch page carries the address, phone (03-3272-7141), hours including the 15:00–16:30 closed window, the access notes and the complete course list with prices. The history page gives the 1930 Ningyōchō founding, the 1932 Ginza move, the 1997 museum, the 2010 Muromachi opening, the 2022 Ginza rebuild and the 2024 Haneda opening, plus the dated list of guests. The FAQ page carries the gluten-free refusal, the shared-fryer statement, the refusal to book egg/wheat/soy/sesame allergy guests, and the vegan/vegetarian/halal accommodation. Tabelog's listing for 銀座 天一 日本橋室町店 confirms the address and coordinates.

gf_cross_contamination.text: 「当店ではすべての食材を同一の揚げ油で調理しております」 — one fryer, every ingredient. The shop states this as its reason for refusing allergy bookings.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tempura is served with tentsuyu built on soy sauce and dashi; no tamari or wheat-free seasoning is mentioned. The batter itself is wheat, which the shop names as the reason gluten-free is impossible.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A vegan course is offered on advance request, but it is fried in the same oil as the seafood — the shop's shared-fryer statement applies to every guest.

staff_allergy_handling.text: 「アレルギーをお持ちのお客様は、ご予約時に必ずお申し付けください… 卵・小麦・大豆・ごまのアレルギーをお持ちのお客様につきましては、安全面を考慮し、ご予約を承ることができかねます」 — they ask you to declare allergies and then decline the booking for the four they cannot handle. Blunt, but honest and safe.
「苦手な食材がございましたら、ご予約時にお知らせください。可能な範囲で、別の食材への変更など対応させていただきます」 — dislikes and substitutions are handled at booking.

positives.text: Vegan, vegetarian and halal courses are all available with advance notice — unusual for a high-end tempura house.

cultural_comfort.note: A formal counter house in an office-district building, open every day but with a 15:00–16:30 break. Book by phone (03-3272-7141) or through Ikyu; same-day cancellation is charged at 100% of the booking, and a seat-only no-show is ¥3,000. Lunch has a table option — the ¥4,950 特製天丼 — which is the low-commitment way in. The site is Japanese with English headings; dietary requests have to be made at the time of booking, not on arrival.

enrich_note: Confirmed. Ten-ichi's own site carries a branch page for 日本橋室町店 with address, phone, hours and prices, and Tabelog lists it at 中央区日本橋室町2-4-3 YUITO 3F with coordinates 35.687411/139.773703, which are the ones used here. The name is written 銀座 天一 on the company's own signage, not 銀座天一, so it has been respaced. The sweep's guess of 三越前駅 was right — the branch connects directly to exit A9. Worth flagging for the app: this is the rare record where the shop publishes an outright gluten-free refusal and says it will not seat a wheat-allergic guest, which is more useful to a celiac reader than a vague 'ask'.

name: 日本橋海鮮丼 つじ半 日本橋本店
address_ja: 〒103-0027 東京都中央区日本橋3-1-15 久栄ビル 1F
cuisine: A twelve-seat counter serving exactly one dish — the 「ぜいたく丼」, a mound of sashimi over rice in four grades (梅 / 竹 / 松 / 特上, the ladder adding crab, ikura and uni as you climb), crowned with a knob of grated wasabi and finished, when you are two-thirds down, by pouring sea-bream dashi over the rest and eating it as chazuke; Tabelog puts the spend at ¥1,000–¥1,999, large rice ¥150 since December 2025
neighborhood: Nihonbashi 3-chōme, on the Yaesu side — 2 min from Nihonbashi Station exit B3 (Ginza, Tōzai and Toei Asakusa lines), 314 m; 5 min from Tokyo Station's Yaesu north exit, 6 min from Kyōbashi
hours_raw: 10:00～22:30（L.O.22:00）　定休日：不定休（年末年始を除く）　※お席の予約は受付しておりません／We don't accept reservations at any store
gf_detail: Nothing on this menu is safe and nothing is offered to make it so. A kaisen-don is dressed with soy sauce or a soy-based tare — wheat soy sauce by default in Japan — and the shop's own selling point is the finish, in which sea-bream dashi is poured over the remaining rice; dashi bases of that kind are normally seasoned with soy as well. There is no allergen page, no tamari, no substitution offer and no reservations at all, so there is not even a booking at which to raise it. Twelve counter seats and a queue is the wrong setting for a detailed allergy conversation.
vegan_detail: The restaurant serves one dish and it is raw fish, with a sea-bream stock to finish. There is no vegan or vegetarian option of any kind.

chef_bio.chef_name: 辻田雄大 (Yūdai Tsujita) and 金子真也 (Shinya Kaneko)
roles: 共同創業者 (co-founders)
辻田: 創業者 of the tsukemen shop つじ田
金子: 創業者 of 日本橋 天丼 金子半之助
chef_bio.origin: Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku — the first shop, opened 13 September 2012
chef_bio.background: Tsujihan is a collaboration between two men who between them already owned two of Nihonbashi's queueing institutions, and the name says so: つじ (from Tsujita's tsukemen shop つじ田) plus 半 (from Kaneko's tendon shop 金子半之助). The shop's own account is that Tsujita Yūdai and Kaneko Shinya were friends from childhood who used to say they would open something together one day. As students they ate, most days and without knowing what it was worth, the kaisen-don that Kaneko's father served at his kappō restaurant. They went their separate ways and each built his own business — Tsujita becoming a name in the tsukemen world, Kaneko in tendon — but neither could forget that bowl, and they decided to open a shop dedicated to it. The first attempt ran straight into the cost of the fish; rather than compromise the contents they took the problem to the Hokkaidō seafood company Kyokuichi, who agreed with what they were trying to do, and it was that supply relationship that let them serve the bowl at the price they wanted. The result opened in Nihonbashi in September 2012 and has queued ever since; there are now branches at Muromachi, Kagurazaka, Tokyo Midtown, Akasaka, Fujimi and several LaLaport malls, plus Taiwan and Hong Kong. The Honten takes no reservations, at any branch, as a matter of policy.
chef_bio.philosophy: One bowl, done properly, at a price that does not insult it — 「もっと安く、同じ品質の物を提供できないか」, the question that sent them to a Hokkaidō fish supplier rather than to cheaper fish.
chef_bio.specialty: ぜいたく丼 in four grades, finished as sea-bream dashi chazuke.

anecdotes.text: The name is a portmanteau of the founders' own shops: つじ田, Tsujita's tsukemen house, and 金子半之助, Kaneko's tendon house.
The bowl they serve is the one Kaneko's father used to make at his kappō restaurant, which the two of them ate almost daily as students without realising what it was worth.
When the fish costs made the bowl impossible at the price they wanted, they took the problem to the Hokkaidō seafood company Kyokuichi, who backed the idea — that partnership is why the price holds.
The free large-rice service, a fixture for years, ended on 30 November 2025 because of the rice price; it is now ¥150.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tsujihan-jp.com carries the founding story in the founders' own words, the no-reservations policy in Japanese and English, the branch list with addresses and hours (Honten 10:00–22:30, L.O. 22:00, 不定休), and the November 2025 notice ending free large rice. Tabelog's Honten page gives the address 中央区日本橋3-1-15 久栄ビル1F, the coordinates used here, the 314 m distance from Nihonbashi Station, the opening date of 13 September 2012, 12 counter seats, cash only, all non-smoking, and the note that the menu is the four grades of ぜいたく丼 with the contents changing by season. Gnavi and Hot Pepper corroborate the address and the dish names.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: A kaisen-don is seasoned with soy sauce, and the house finish pours sea-bream dashi over the rice; neither is described as wheat-free and no tamari is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Single-item menu, all of it raw fish, finished with fish stock.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No reservations are taken at any branch — 「お席の予約は受付しておりません」 — so there is no booking at which to declare an allergy, and the twelve-seat counter runs a queue.

cultural_comfort.note: Twelve counter seats, no reservations, a queue most of the day, and Tabelog records the Honten as cash only — no cards, no e-money, no QR payment — so bring notes. Ordering is a single word: 梅, 竹, 松 or 特上. Children over primary-school age are fine, takeaway and delivery exist, the room is all non-smoking. Open 10:00 to 22:30 with irregular closures, so check before a special trip. Almost no Japanese is needed, but almost none is spoken either.

name: 銀座 朧月
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座6-4-13 浅黄ビル 1F
cuisine: An eight-seat counter doing thick-noodle tsukemen in a double broth of pork bone and dried fish — the shop's own line is 「濃すぎずあっさりしすぎず」, rich without being sludge — alongside the 中華そば it opened with and a rotating seasonal bowl (a 辛つけ麺 and a summer cold ramen both turn up in 2026 reviews); roughly ¥1,200–¥1,550 a bowl, Tabelog's band ¥1,000–¥1,999
neighborhood: Ginza 6-chōme, on the Shinbashi side — 3 min from Ginza Station (Ginza, Marunouchi and Hibiya lines), 263 m; 8 min from JR Yūrakuchō
gf_detail: Wheat is the point of the dish. Reviewers single out the noodles as 「小麦の風味満点なもちもち極太ストレート麺」 — thick straight noodles made to taste of wheat — and the dipping broth is a pork-and-fish tare seasoned with soy sauce. No gluten-free noodle, no tamari and no allergen information is published on Tabelog, on the shop's Instagram or anywhere else found. Eight counter seats with a queue outside is also the wrong room for a detailed allergy negotiation.
vegan_detail: The whole menu is built on a 豚骨と魚介のWスープ — pork bones plus dried fish. There is no vegetable broth and no vegan bowl.

chef_bio.background: The owner's name is not published: the shop has no website, and neither its Tabelog listing nor its Instagram carries a chef's name, so none is asserted here. What is documented is the trajectory. Oborozuki built its reputation as a queueing tsukemen shop and has been a repeat Tabelog Ramen Hyakumeiten selection — reviewers in 2026 tag it 元百名店 and 百名店候補 and it holds a 3.66 aggregate over nearly a thousand reviews. On 5 September 2024 it moved into a new address in Ginza 6-chōme; Tabelog carries the relocation flag and keeps the pre-move listing separately. The new room is deliberately small and un-ramen-like — eight seats at a counter, described by the shop as 「小料理屋を思わせるカウンターのみのおしゃれ空間」, a space closer to a small kappō counter than a noodle bar, and explicitly friendly to solo diners. The house style is a double broth of pork bone and dried seafood that the shop positions between the two extremes of the genre, served with very thick chewy straight noodles; the 中華そば has been on the menu since the shop opened and there are seasonal limited bowls. The tsukemen is sold nationwide as a chilled mail-order kit through Takumen.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「濃すぎずあっさりしすぎずのバランス」 — a tsukemen broth thick enough to coat the noodle but not so heavy you cannot finish it.
chef_bio.specialty: 特製つけ麺 — pork-and-fish double broth with very thick straight noodles; also 中華そば and seasonal limited bowls.

anecdotes.text: The shop moved to its Ginza 6-chōme address on 5 September 2024; Tabelog still keeps the pre-relocation listing as a separate page.
Only eight seats, all at a counter, and the shop describes the room as feeling like a 小料理屋 rather than a ramen shop — solo diners are the expected customer.
Reviewers file it under 元百名店 / 百名店候補 — a former Tabelog Ramen Hyakumeiten pick — and it carries a 3.66 aggregate across 997 reviews as of August 2026.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog's listing is the primary source and is shop-verified (公式): address 中央区銀座6-4-13 浅黄ビル1F, phone 03-6280-6166, the full weekday-by-weekday hours, 予約不可, eight counter seats, all non-smoking, cards/e-money/QR all accepted, and the shop's own PR copy describing the double broth and the 中華そば. soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping broth is a soy-seasoned pork-and-fish tare; no tamari or wheat-free option is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork bone and dried fish are the base of every bowl on the menu.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No reservations are taken, so there is no booking at which to declare an allergy.

cultural_comfort.note: Eight counter seats, no reservations, expect to queue — but unusually for a ramen shop it takes cards, transport IC, iD, QUICPay and every major QR payment, so you are not hunting for cash. All non-smoking. Solo diners are the norm and the shop says so. No English is advertised; ordering is a one-word transaction and there is a photo-heavy Instagram to point at.

address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座3-11-6 鈴木ビル 1F
cuisine: Ten counter seats behind a ticket machine, serving one thing very well: a 中華そば at ¥1,200 (large portion at the same price) in a clear shio broth of pork bone and dried sardine, filled so high that reviewers warn the bowl is about to breach, with soft wide-ish noodles and a generous pile of pork; occasional limited bowls including a summer 冷やし
neighborhood: Ginza 3-chōme by the Kabuki-za — 1 min from Higashi-Ginza exit A7 (Toei Asakusa line), 3 min from the Hibiya line side, 214 m from the station
gf_detail: Wheat noodles in a soy-and-salt seasoned broth, ordered from a ticket machine with no allergen labelling and no reservation at which to ask. Nothing gluten-free is offered, nothing is claimed, and there is no route to a safe order here.
vegan_detail: The broth is pork bone and niboshi (dried sardine) and the bowl comes loaded with chāshū. No vegan or vegetarian option exists.

chef_bio.chef_name: 「はるちゃん」 (the owner-chef is known publicly only by this name)
roles: 店主 (owner-chef)
chef_bio.background: This is the second shop of the Shimbashi ramen bar はるちゃんラーメン, which built its name on a clear salt-seasoned 中華そば and picked up a Michelin Bib Gourmand; the Ginza branch opened on 16 July 2024, a minute from the Kabuki-za, and appears in the Michelin Guide Tokyo's ramen listings in its own right. Michelin's entry describes the owner as 「はるちゃん」 and the bowl as a 塩味の中華そば on a clear broth of pork bone and dried sardine, served filled to the brim — the last part is not a flourish, it is the shop's signature and every review mentions carrying the bowl carefully. Japanese ramen writers file the style under 「ちゃん系」, a small recognised lineage of clear shio bowls with soft flat noodles and a heavy hand with the pork, and this shop is one of the names the genre is built around. Ordering is by ticket machine before you queue. It is not a cheap bowl by Tokyo standards — ¥1,200 for a plain 中華そば drew comment even from admiring reviewers — but the shop serves the large size at the same price. The owner's real name has not been published in any source found and is not asserted here.
chef_bio.philosophy: One bowl, clear shio, filled to the rim.
chef_bio.specialty: 中華そば ¥1,200 — clear pork-and-niboshi shio broth, soft noodles, generous chāshū; large portion at no extra charge.

anecdotes.text: Opened 16 July 2024 as the second branch of the Shimbashi original, a minute from the Kabuki-za.
The shop opens at 09:00 on weekdays — ramen for breakfast, and one of very few Ginza kitchens serving anything at that hour.
The bowl is filled so close to the rim that reviewers write about the surface tension: 「波々入って気を付けないと決壊しそうなスープ量」.
Large is served at the same ¥1,200 as regular.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog gives the address 中央区銀座3-11-6 鈴木ビル1F, phone 03-6260-6088, the 16 July 2024 opening date, weekday 09:00–21:00 and weekend 11:00–21:00 hours, 予約不可, ten counter seats, all non-smoking, cards, e-money and QR accepted, and the coordinates used here. The Michelin Guide carries a Tokyo entry for 銀座はるちゃんラーメン / Ginza HARU CHAN Ramen describing the owner as はるちゃん and the bowl as a clear pork-and-niboshi shio 中華そば. The shop's Instagram (@haruchan_ginza) lists the address and hours and cites the Michelin Guide Tokyo 2026. Several Japanese ramen blogs date the opening, place it one minute from Higashi-Ginza exit A7, and identify it as the second branch of the Bib Gourmand Shimbashi shop.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One noodle boiler, wheat noodles all day, ten seats. No separation is possible and none is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: A shio broth in Japan is still salted with a soy-based tare unless stated otherwise; nothing here is described as wheat-free and no tamari is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork bone and dried sardine broth with chāshū on top — animal products in the base, not just the garnish.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Ticket machine ordering, no reservations, and a queue on the pavement — there is no point in the transaction at which an allergy conversation naturally happens.

cultural_comfort.note: Buy a ticket from the machine first, then join the queue — the standard Tokyo ramen protocol, and the machine does the talking for you. Ten counter seats, all non-smoking, cards, e-money and QR payment all accepted. Open from 09:00 on weekdays, which makes it a rare option before the Kabuki-za matinée. No English signage is advertised; the menu is essentially one item.

enrich_note: Confirmed and pinned at 中央区銀座3-11-6 鈴木ビル1F, coordinates 35.670855/139.768842 from Tabelog; opened 16 July 2024. The sweep's 'Higashi-Ginza Station' was right — the shop is 214 m from it. Two claims in the light record needed care. The sweep called it 'Michelin-recognized': Michelin does carry a guide page for it, and Japanese secondary sources describe it as a Bib Gourmand in the Michelin Guide Tokyo 2026 alongside the Shimbashi original, but Michelin's own page returned HTTP 403 to two direct fetch attempts (curl and a second fetch path), so the Bib Gourmand tier itself rests on the shop's Instagram and Japanese ramen press rather than on a page I opened — hence chef_bio confidence medium. The sweep also called it 'run by chef Haru-chan', which is as much as anyone publishes: no real name appears in any source found, so none has been invented.

name: 煉瓦亭
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座3-5-16 煉瓦亭ビル
cuisine: The 1895 Ginza yōshoku house where much of the genre is said to have been settled — 元祖ポークカツレツ with shredded raw cabbage and Worcestershire rather than demi-glace, 元祖オムライス, 明治誕生オムライス, 元祖ハヤシライス, prawn and winter oyster fries, consommé and potage; Tabelog's declared spend is ¥1,000–¥1,999 at lunch and ¥2,000–¥2,999 at night, with reviewers actually paying ¥3,000–¥3,999
neighborhood: Ginza 3-chōme, behind Wakō on Gas-tō-dōri — 3 min from Ginza Station exits A10 or B1 (Ginza, Marunouchi and Hibiya lines), 195 m
hours_raw: 月・火・水・木・金・土・祝日 11:15～15:00（L.O.14:00）／17:30～21:00（L.O.20:00）　日曜日 定休　※夜は日によって変動があるためお問合せください
gf_detail: Yōshoku is a wheat cuisine and this is the house that made it one. The signature cutlets are breaded in flour, egg and panko; the hayashi rice is bound with a demi-glace, which is a roux; the Worcestershire sauce poured over the cutlet is itself normally wheat-containing; there is macaroni, spaghetti, gratin and bread on the same menu. The kitchen publishes no allergen information, takes no reservations, and has no website on which to state a policy. Nothing here is safe for a celiac.
vegan_detail: A meat-and-egg menu almost end to end — cutlets, omelettes, hashed beef, prawn and oyster fries. The only meatless items are a handful of side salads and the potage, and neither the stock nor the dressings are described as animal-free.

chef_bio.chef_name: 木田明利 (Akitoshi Kida), fourth-generation owner; founded by 山本音次郎 (Otojirō Yamamoto)
roles: 四代目オーナー (fourth-generation owner) — 木田明利
創業者 (founder, 1895) — 山本音次郎
二代目 — 木田元次郎
三代目 — 木田孝一
chef_bio.origin: Ginza 3-chōme, Chūō-ku — the shop has been on this block since 1895; the present building dates from 1964
chef_bio.background: Rengatei opened in 1895 and is the restaurant most often credited with inventing Japanese yōshoku as a category — Ginza's own shop directory calls it the first place in Japan to be described as a 洋食屋. The claims made for it are large: that the second-generation owner Kida Motsujirō devised the modern pork cutlet, omurice, oyster and prawn fry, hayashi rice, and even the habit of serving rice on a flat plate rather than in a bowl so that it could be eaten with a fork. The house's own explanations are pleasingly practical rather than romantic. Rice on a plate came from customers who wanted rice rather than bread with their Western food and could not manage a chawan with a knife and fork — which is where the Japanese habit of eating rice off the back of the fork is said to have started. The shredded raw cabbage beside the cutlet was a wartime expedient: with the cooks conscripted for the Russo-Japanese War there was nobody left to prepare hot vegetables, so they took the idea from overnight-pickled cabbage, cut it fine, and found it was cheap and went well with sauce. And the cutlet got Worcestershire instead of demi-glace because Japanese diners found the French sauce heavy. Omurice began as staff food — beaten egg, minced meat, onion and rice cooked quickly in a pan — and went on the menu because customers asked for it. It should be said plainly that these origin stories are contested: the Japanese Wikipedia article notes that since 2017 several published studies have argued Rengatei did not in fact invent these dishes, and the third-generation owner's claim on hayashi rice concedes that Maruzen in Nihonbashi got there first with a different version. What is not contested is the continuity. The building is the 1964 one, the fourth generation is behind it, Yamamoto Masuhiro's 1982 Tokyo restaurant guide gave it three stars, Tabelog has picked it for the yōshoku Hyakumeiten in 2020, 2022 and 2025, and in March 2023 President Yoon Suk-yeol of South Korea and Prime Minister Kishida ate there together after their summit.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「日本の洋食はここから始まった」 — the house line. Western technique bent to what Japanese diners actually wanted: rice on a plate, raw cabbage instead of hot vegetables, Worcestershire instead of demi-glace.
chef_bio.specialty: 元祖ポークカツレツ, 元祖オムライス and 明治誕生オムライス, 元祖ハヤシライス, カキフライ in winter.

anecdotes.text: The shredded raw cabbage that now comes with every tonkatsu in Japan is said to have started here as a labour-saving substitute when the cooks were conscripted for the Russo-Japanese War.
Serving rice on a flat plate — and therefore eating it off the back of a fork — is attributed to this shop, after customers asked for rice instead of bread with Western dishes.
Omurice started as the staff meal and went on the menu because customers kept asking for it.
On the evening of 16 March 2023, South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol and Prime Minister Kishida Fumio held their post-summit dinner here.
Not everyone accepts the origin stories: several studies published since 2017 dispute that Rengatei invented these dishes at all.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog's listing gives the address 中央区銀座3-5-16, the 1895 opening date, phone 03-3561-3882, hours 11:15–15:00 (L.O. 14:00) and 17:30–21:00 (L.O. 20:00) with Sunday closed, 予約不可, cash only, 110 seats including tatami, all non-smoking, no dress code, children welcome, the full 73-item menu list, and 洋食百名店 selections for 2020, 2022 and 2025. Ginza's official shop directory (ginza.jp) confirms the 1895 founding, the address, the phone and the hours, and describes it as the first restaurant in Japan called a 洋食屋. Japanese Wikipedia supplies the ownership line — founder 山本音次郎, second 木田元次郎, third 木田孝一, fourth 木田明利 — the 1964 building, the 1982 three-star rating in Yamamoto Masuhiro's guide, the 2023 Yoon–Kishida dinner, and the scholarly dispute over the invention claims.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A 110-seat kitchen breading and deep-frying cutlets, prawns and oysters all service, with pasta and gratin on the same menu. There is no separated line and none is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The sauce on the house cutlet is Worcestershire rather than demi-glace — a deliberate choice made generations ago — and commercial Worcestershire in Japan is not wheat-free. The hayashi rice is demi-glace, i.e. a flour roux.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Meat, egg and seafood run through effectively the entire menu; the shared fryer handles prawns and oysters.

staff_allergy_handling.text: 予約不可 — no reservations at all, so there is no advance conversation to be had, and the shop publishes no website or allergen sheet.

cultural_comfort.note: No reservations and no cards, e-money or QR payment — cash only, which surprises people in Ginza, so come with notes. Expect to queue at lunch; 110 seats over more than one floor, including tatami rooms, all non-smoking, no dress code, children welcome. Closed Sundays, with a break between lunch and 17:30 and evening hours that the shop itself says vary by day. The menu is long, old-fashioned and largely in Japanese, though the dish names are the familiar yōshoku ones and there are photographs to point at.

enrich_note: NAME CORRECTION. The light record read 「レンガ亭」 in katakana. No Ginza business writes itself that way: the shop, its building, its Instagram handle, Ginza's official shop directory and Tabelog all use the kanji 煉瓦亭 (read Rengatei), at 中央区銀座3-5-16, and the katakana form appears only as Tabelog's furigana gloss レンガテイ. Enriched under the kanji name, pinned at Tabelog's 35.672760/139.766021 — about 200 m north-east of the sweep's Ginza centroid. Everything else in the light record checks out: Ginza, Ginza Station, yōshoku. One caution carried into the bio rather than the summary line: the shop's famous 元祖 claims (pork cutlet, omurice, hayashi rice, rice on a plate) are disputed in print by Japanese food historians since 2017, so they are reported here as the house's claims, not as fact.

name: てんぷら 近藤
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F
cuisine: Two-Michelin-star tempura on the ninth floor of a Ginza block, fried by Kondō Fumio himself at lunch and dinner — the batter is thinned to the edge of nothing so the ingredient shows through, and vegetables are treated as the equal of seafood, most famously a sweet potato cut like a tree stump and fried slowly for about thirty minutes; lunch courses 菫 ¥13,200 and 椿 ¥16,500, dinner 藤 ¥22,000 / 楓 ¥27,500 / 蓬 ¥33,000, tax included
neighborhood: Ginza 5-chōme, ninth floor of the Sakaguchi building — 5 min from Ginza Station (Ginza, Marunouchi and Hibiya lines)
gf_detail: The shop's own opening statement is that its tempura is light 「小麦粉で作る天ぷらの衣が油を吸い過ぎないから」 — because the wheat-flour coating does not drink oil. Wheat batter is the whole technique here, everything goes through the same pot, and tentsuyu is a soy-and-dashi dip. No allergen page, no gluten-free claim, no substitution offer appears on tempura-kondo.com in any of its five languages. There is no version of this meal without wheat.
vegan_detail: Kondō is the chef who insisted vegetables belonged in a serious tempura course — he contracts directly with growers after tasting on the farm, and the sweet potato is his signature dish — so a vegetable-led course is genuinely part of the house repertoire rather than a concession. But that is not the same as vegan: tempura batter is normally bound with egg, the pot is shared with prawns and fish all service, and the standard tsuyu is a bonito dashi. Nothing about vegan or vegetarian handling is published anywhere on the site. It is a reasonable thing to raise when you book, through the multilingual reservation desk, but it has not been promised.

roles: 店主・料理長 (owner-chef)
元「てんぷらと和食 山の上」料理長 (former head chef, Tempura & Washoku Yamanoue)
chef_bio.background: Kondō went straight from high school into Yamanoue, the tempura and washoku restaurant in the Hilltop Hotel, and was made head chef there at twenty-three — an absurd age for the job — staying more than twenty years before leaving to open his own counter in Ginza in June 1991. He is generally credited with two things. The first is thinning the batter: he threw out the idea of a thick coating and took it as close to nothing as it will go, so that the colour and smell of the ingredient come through and the piece does not absorb oil. The second is vegetables. Edomae tempura had meant seafood, with fried vegetables regarded as delicatessen food and beneath a serious restaurant; Kondō argued that no cuisine in the world ignores the vegetables of its own country, and that if tempura was ever going to stand beside sushi as a representative Japanese cuisine it needed a course that could hold a diner's attention without leaning entirely on fish. He buys by going to the farm and tasting before he contracts, and asks growers for 「本当のもの、最高のもの」. His signature is a sweet potato cut into a stump more than ten centimetres thick and fried slowly for around half an hour, on the reasoning that a baked sweet potato is delicious, so a tempura ought to beat one. He also describes tempura as fundamentally a steaming technique rather than a frying one: the batter seals the ingredient, the residual heat keeps cooking it after it leaves the oil, and the timing has to account for that. After more than fifty years in the trade he still stands at the counter for both services. In 2019 he became the first tempura chef to receive 現代の名工, the government's Contemporary Master Craftsman award; in 2023 he was the first tempura chef given Michelin's Mentor Chef Award; and the restaurant has held two Michelin stars continuously since 2008.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「天ぷらは、料理人がゲストをお招きする料理」 — tempura is a dish with which the cook invites the guest in. Batter as thin as it will go, and vegetables treated as seriously as fish.
chef_bio.specialty: The sweet potato — a stump over 10 cm thick, fried around thirty minutes — plus seasonal Edomae seafood, in courses of ¥13,200 to ¥33,000.

anecdotes.text: He was made head chef of Yamanoue at twenty-three and stayed in the post for over twenty years before going out on his own in 1991.
The sweet potato came from a simple challenge to himself: baked sweet potato is delicious, so make a tempura that beats it. The answer was a stump-sized cut fried for about half an hour.
He argues tempura is really a steaming dish — 「天ぷらとは熱と水分で食材の旨味をうまく引き出す蒸し物」 — and that you have to allow for the carry-over cooking after the piece leaves the oil.
First tempura chef to be named 現代の名工 (2019) and first to receive Michelin's Mentor Chef Award (2023).
The house asks guests not to arrive wearing strong perfume, and to phone if they will be more than fifteen minutes late.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tempura-kondo.com is the primary source and runs in Japanese, English, traditional and simplified Chinese and Korean. It carries the chef's dated biography, his statements on batter, on vegetables and on tempura as steaming, the sweet-potato account, the address 中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F, the phone number, the seating (two counters of 12 and 8), the current and post-September-2026 hours, the full course prices, and the awards including two Michelin stars every year since 2008. Tabelog corroborates the address, gives the June 1991 opening date, 20 seats, all non-smoking, cards accepted, the two-sitting service pattern, Sunday closure with an occasional Wednesday, and records Tabelog Award Bronze for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2025 and 2026 plus 天ぷら百名店 selections in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One pot, one counter, every course fried in sequence in front of you. There is no separated line and the shop makes no claim of one.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The batter is explicitly wheat flour, described by the chef as the reason the tempura is light; tentsuyu is a soy-and-dashi dip with no wheat-free version offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetables are fried in the same oil as prawns and fish throughout the service, and tempura batter is normally egg-bound.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Nothing about allergies is published. Reservations are handled in Japanese by phone or form for domestic guests and through the official multilingual desk (My Concierge Japan) for overseas guests, which is the practical channel for raising a dietary need in writing before you arrive.

positives.text: A vegetable-heavy repertoire by design, with produce contracted farm by farm — the raw material for a meatless course exists here in a way it does not at most tempura counters, even though no vegan handling is promised.

cultural_comfort.note: Reservation-only in practice, in fixed sittings — from September 2026 lunch at 11:30 or 13:30 with two hours at the table, dinner at 17:00 or 19:30 with two and a half. Overseas guests book through the restaurant's official multilingual desk rather than by phone, since the phone line is Japanese only; the website itself runs in five languages. Two counters, 20 seats, all non-smoking, cards accepted. Be on time — more than fifteen minutes late requires a call — and the house asks you not to wear heavy perfume, which tells you how seriously the room takes smell. Change fees apply on the cancellation scale from the moment you alter a booking.

enrich_note: Confirmed and pinned at 中央区銀座5-5-13 坂口ビル9F, coordinates 35.671178/139.763187 from Tabelog; the shop's own site carries the same address. The light record's two claims both check out but need slight correction. 'Tabelog Award 2026 Bronze' is right — Tabelog lists Bronze for 2026, and also for 2025, 2020, 2019 and 2018 — but the bigger fact the sweep missed is two Michelin stars every year since 2008, which the shop states on its own front page. 'Seasonal Edomae special' undersells the house: the thing Kondō is actually known for is having forced vegetables into serious tempura, and the signature dish is a sweet potato. Hours are recorded in full because they change in September 2026: the site publishes both the current and the incoming timetable.

name: 銀座 玉ゐ
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座6-8-7 交詢ビル4F
cuisine: The Ginza room of the Nihonbashi anago house Tamai, on the fourth floor of the Kōjun building — the branch-only 「いかだ箱めし」 (¥3,500) lays three medium conger, simmered then glazed and grilled, side by side like a raft over the rice; Ginza-only kaiseki courses run 梅 ¥7,000, 竹 ¥9,000 and 松 ¥10,800, the last taking in anago tataki with ponzu, shirayaki and tempura
neighborhood: Ginza 6-chōme, in the Kōjun building on Suzuran-dōri (Barneys New York is on the ground floor) — 3 min from Ginza Station exit A1, 227 m
gf_detail: Same kitchen policy as the Nihonbashi flagship, and the same problem: the house 「つめだれ」 that goes over every box of rice is sugar and wheat soy sauce, and the Ginza courses add an explicit 揚げ物 course — the 松 course names tempura outright. No tamari, no allergen sheet and no wheat-free preparation appears on anago-tamai.com. A celiac has nothing to order here.
vegan_detail: Every course and every à la carte item is conger eel, and the optional finishing stock is boiled from grilled anago bones. Nothing vegan is offered.

roles: 創業者・代表取締役 (founder / representative director of Tamai, per the 2022 Chūō ward interview)
元江戸前寿司職人 (former Edomae sushi chef)
chef_bio.origin: Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku — the parent shop opened there in June 2005
chef_bio.background: Ginza Tamai is a branch of the Nihonbashi anago specialist 日本橋 玉ゐ, founded in June 2005 by a group of Edomae sushi chefs after a customer at their sushi counter said Tokyo needed a shop dedicated to conger. The name comes from Tamai-san, a senior colleague among the founders. The house buys only wild anago, in season, through Toyosu, following the run from the Inland Sea in spring to Edomae in early summer, Jōban and Sendai in late summer and Tsushima in winter, and it deliberately takes the sizes the rest of the trade cannot use — the 70 cm, 300 g fish and the small 「めそ」 — because tempura shops want 120 g eels and sushi counters 150–180 g. Michelin gave the group a Bib Gourmand in 2015. This branch is the group's dress-up room. It sits on the fourth floor of the Kōjun building in Ginza 6-chōme, on the site where Fukuzawa Yukichi founded the Kōjunsha in the Meiji era — Japan's first members' club for politicians and businessmen — and the shop mentions that history on its own page. It is the only branch to take lunch reservations as well as dinner, the only one with private rooms, and the only one with its own kaiseki courses; conversely the group's standard あなご会席 cannot be ordered here. Its exclusive dish is the いかだ箱めし, three medium conger simmered and then finished as kabayaki and laid out like a raft, chosen for a good fat content and few small bones.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「平成生まれの老舗」 — build an old shop from scratch. Wild eel only, in season, and the sizes nobody else competes for.
chef_bio.specialty: いかだ箱めし ¥3,500 (this branch only) and the Ginza-only 梅・竹・松 kaiseki courses.

anecdotes.text: The building is the Kōjun building, on the site where Fukuzawa Yukichi founded the Kōjunsha — Japan's first members' club for politicians and businessmen. Barneys New York occupies the ground floor; Tamai is on the fourth.
This is the only Tamai branch taking reservations at lunch as well as dinner, and the only one with private rooms — one for four, one for six.
Guests who are not on an evening course pay a ¥500 otōshi as a seat charge.
Raw anago sashimi is served from early July to late September, and only at three of the group's shops — the Honten, Muromachi and here.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: anago-tamai.com's Ginza page carries the address 中央区銀座6-8-7 交詢ビル4F, the phone number 03-6264-6896, the weekday and weekend hours, the 38 seats and two private rooms, the ¥500 otōshi rule, the branch-exclusive いかだ箱めし and the three Ginza-only course menus with prices, plus the Kōjunsha history of the building and turn-by-turn directions from Ginza exit A1. The group's menu page confirms which dishes are branch-exclusive and which are excluded here. Tabelog's 銀座 玉ゐ listing supplies the coordinates used and the 227 m distance from Ginza Station. The Chūō ward tourism association's 2022 interview with representative 佐藤裕二 supplies the group's founding, sourcing and the confirmation that the house tare is sugar and soy sauce.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The Ginza courses include a dedicated 揚げ物 course and the 松 course serves tempura; the kitchen fries in wheat batter alongside everything else.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house 「つめだれ」 is 砂糖と醤油 — sugar and wheat soy sauce — and it goes over the eel in every box.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Anago in every dish; the finishing stock is made from grilled anago bones.

positives.text: Unlike the other branches this one takes reservations at both services and has private rooms, so there is at least a booking conversation in which to raise a dietary need — by phone, or through Tabelog, Ikyu, Gurunavi or Hot Pepper.

cultural_comfort.note: 38 seats plus two private rooms (one for four, one for six), fourth floor of the Kōjun building — from Ginza exit A1, turn left at the Manneken waffle shop, up Suzuran-dōri, past Uniqlo, and it is the building on the right with Barneys on the ground floor. Reservations taken for lunch and dinner on 03-6264-6896 or through Tabelog, Ikyu, Gurunavi and Hot Pepper. Guests not taking an evening course pay a ¥500 otōshi. The group's site runs in English, Korean and Chinese.

enrich_note: Confirmed and pinned. This is a real, separately named branch, not a duplicate of the Nihonbashi record earlier in this shard: the operator's own site gives it its own page, its own address at 中央区銀座6-8-7 交詢ビル4F, its own phone number, its own reservation policy and three course menus that cannot be ordered at any other branch — while the group's standard あなご会席 explicitly cannot be ordered here. Coordinates 35.670120/139.762819 are Tabelog's, about 250 m south-west of the sweep's Ginza centroid. The sweep's '3 min walk from Ginza Station' matches the shop's own directions.

name: とんかつ 銀座梅林 本店
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座7-8-1 銀座梅林ビル 地下1階

neighborhood: Ginza 7-chōme on Kōjunsha-dōri, in the basement of the Bairin building — 3 min from Ginza Station exit A2, walking from the Ginza 4-chōme crossing towards Shinbashi; 289 m from the station
hours_raw: 11:30開店～20:00ラストオーダー（21:00閉店）　途中の休憩時間はございません／定休日もございません（1月1日を除く）
gf_detail: Everything on the plate is wheat. The cutlets are floured, egged and crumbed in a fresh panko the shop developed itself; the katsudon tare is a soy-seasoned pork-and-onion stock; and the house's proudest possession is its own 中濃ソース, a Worcestershire-type sauce invented by the founder — a category that is not wheat-free in Japan. There is no allergen page, no reservation at which to ask and no substitution offered. Nothing here is safe for a celiac.
vegan_detail: Pork, prawn and egg run through the entire menu. The only non-animal element is the shredded cabbage and the rice; the katsudon tare is a meat stock and even the miso bowl will be dashi-based. No vegan or vegetarian dish is offered.

chef_bio.chef_name: 澁谷信勝 (Nobukatsu Shibuya), founder — now in its third generation
roles: 創業者 (founder, 1927)
元薬剤師 (a trained pharmacist before he was a restaurateur)
chef_bio.origin: Ginza, Chūō-ku — open on the same street since 1927
chef_bio.background: Ginza Bairin opened in 1927 as the first tonkatsu specialist in Ginza, and the founder Shibuya Nobukatsu spent his first years redesigning the dish rather than serving it. Fillet cutlets at the time were opened flat and fried whole; he cut them into bite-sized pieces instead and sold them as 「ひと口カツ」, which is the shop's oldest claim to fame. Dissatisfied with the sauces then available he used his training — he had been a pharmacist — to formulate his own 中濃ソース, thickened and sweetened with apple and onion, and that sauce is still sold over the counter to take home. For katsudon he refused the usual bonito-dashi base used by soba shops and built a tare instead on a stock simmered from pork sinew and onion, finished sweet in the Kantō manner. Later came a fillet katsu sandwich on white bread and the スペシャルカツ丼, which sets a second egg on top of the finished bowl. The shop's nickname, 珍豚美人 — read *chintonshan*, a pun that reads roughly as 'rare pork beauty' and also imitates a shamisen phrase — comes from a piece of calligraphy given to the first owner by the fifth-generation kōdan storyteller Ichiryūsai Teijō, and it is still used affectionately by customers. The house is now in its third generation, which took the brand abroad: a food-court counter at Haneda Terminal 1 in December 2005, a restaurant in Waikiki in May 2007, and later Seoul. Sourcing is specific: Kagoshima kurobuta among the pork, a fresh panko with the sugar dialled down so it does not colour before the meat is done, cottonseed-oil-based frying fat, and Yamagata Tsuyahime rice, refilled free. The Ginza flagship moved into the basement of its own building in July 2021 — the same street, one floor down from the shopfront regulars remember.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「銀座のおもてなしの心」 — Ginza hospitality, applied to a cutlet. Control every component yourself, including the sauce, the crumb and the frying fat.
chef_bio.specialty: 元祖ひと口カツ (bite-sized fillet cutlet), the katsudon on a pork-and-onion tare, and the house 中濃ソース.

anecdotes.text: The founder was a pharmacist, and used that training to formulate the shop's own tonkatsu sauce — apple and onion for body and sweetness. It is still sold to take home.
The katsudon tare deliberately avoids the bonito dashi that soba shops use, and is built instead on a stock simmered from pork sinew and onion.
The shop's nickname 珍豚美人 (chintonshan) comes from calligraphy presented to the first owner by the kōdan storyteller Ichiryūsai Teijō V, a friend of the founder.
Rice is Yamagata Tsuyahime and refills are free — the shop says so on its own menu page.
No reservations, in Japanese and in English on the front page: 「銀座梅林ではお席のご予約は受けておりません」 / 'We do not take reservations.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ginzabairin.com is the operator's own site. Its shop page gives the address 中央区銀座7-8-1 銀座梅林ビル地下1階, the phone 03-3571-0350, hours of 11:30–20:00 (L.O.) with no break and no closing day except 1 January, and directions from Ginza exit A2. The about page carries the 1927 founding, the founder's name and pharmacist background, the ひと口カツ and 中濃ソース inventions, the katsudon tare, the 珍豚美人 nickname and its origin, and the Haneda (2005), Waikiki (2007) and Seoul expansions under the third generation. The menu page lists every set with April 2024 prices and details the pork, panko, frying oil, sauce, rice and cabbage sourcing. Tabelog's current listing confirms the basement address, gives coordinates, records the July 2021 opening of the present premises, 28 seats, all non-smoking, wheelchair access, cards and transport IC accepted, and 予約不可.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A single tonkatsu fryer running breaded pork and prawns all day. No separation is claimed and none is plausible.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house sauce is a 中濃ソース of the Worcestershire family, which in Japan is not wheat-free, and the katsudon tare is soy-seasoned. Neither is offered in a wheat-free form.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork, egg and prawn throughout; the katsudon tare is itself a pork stock.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No reservations are taken at all, so there is no advance channel; the shop does say it will adjust portion sizes and combine à la carte items into a set on request, which shows a willingness to flex — but on quantity, not on allergens.

positives.text: The frying fat is a cottonseed-oil blend rather than lard, and the shop names it — useful information if you avoid pork fat for non-allergy reasons, though the cutlet itself is pork.

cultural_comfort.note: No reservations — you queue and are seated in order, and the shop asks that your whole party be present before it seats you. 28 seats in the basement (a 12-seat counter plus four tables of four), all non-smoking, wheelchair accessible, cards and transport IC accepted, easy for a solo diner. Open 11:30 to 20:00 last order with no afternoon break, every day except 1 January. There is an English page on the site, takeaway bento can be ordered ahead on 03-3571-0350, and you can mix à la carte items into a set or ask for a smaller portion.

name: 銀座 四代目 高橋屋 銀座店
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座4-12-1 VORT銀座イーストⅡビル 4F
cuisine: Unagi killed and split to order at the counter — a quarter of each fish goes to shirayaki so you taste it unglazed, the rest is grilled over binchōtan and lacquered with the house tare; 割きたてうな重御膳 ¥8,800 is the one people come for, with うな丼御膳 ¥5,800, 特上うな重御膳 ¥7,800, a 天然うな重御膳 at ¥19,800 using wild eel, and a 四代目 kaiseki course at ¥24,800 that ends with the eel box; tax included, no service charge
neighborhood: Ginza 4-chōme, fourth floor of the VORT Ginza East II building next to the Kabuki-za stage door — 1 min from Higashi-Ginza (Toei Asakusa and Hibiya lines, exit A7, 103 m), 4 min from Ginza Station exit A13
gf_detail: The kabayaki is out — the house tare is a soy, mirin and sugar glaze and the shop treats it as an heirloom, so it will not be changed. But this is one of the few records in this shard where a real conversation is possible. A quarter of every eel is served 白焼き, grilled plain without tare, and it comes with 生わさび, freshly grated wasabi rather than the tubed paste that often carries wheat starch. The shop invites dietary discussion in writing on its own listing — 「うなぎが苦手、うな重がダメな方、遠慮なくご相談下さい」 — takes reservations, seats only fourteen, and has English-speaking staff and an English menu. None of that is a gluten-free guarantee: the same grill and the same kitchen handle tare-basted eel all service, the miso soup will be a katsuo dashi seasoned with soy, and no allergen policy is published. Raise it when you book and ask specifically about shirayaki, salt and the soup.
vegan_detail: A dedicated eel house that kills and splits live fish at the counter as its selling point, seasoned with katsuo dashi and kombu. There is no vegan or vegetarian option.

chef_bio.chef_name: 高橋明宏 (Akihiro Takahashi), fourth-generation head chef
roles: 四代目 料理長 — 高橋明宏
取締役 総料理長 — 綾ゆうき
執行役 料理長 — 田中翔児
取締役 総支配人 — 高田啓史
chef_bio.origin: The family trade is older than the Ginza address: the house traces itself through 紫雲亭 (founded around 1820), renamed 藤喜紫雲亭 around 1870, and 高橋屋 from around 1890
chef_bio.background: Takahashiya counts 150 years as a kappō and, if you follow the line back through its two earlier names, close to two hundred. The Ginza room is the newest expression of it — opened on 14 August 2021 on the fourth floor of a building beside the Kabuki-za stage door, with the company also running shops at Sugito in Saitama and Kawagoe plus two mail-order operations. The fourth generation's stated project is to bring a revolution to the eel trade while keeping the tradition intact, and the shop is candid that its cooking rests on two other houses: the Mitsui zaibatsu's ryōtei 松の茶屋, and Ginza Kojyu, the two-star Japanese restaurant a few streets west. What that means in practice is an eel restaurant run like a kaiseki house. Live 青うなぎ from Mikawa Isshiki are bought in and split to order — the shop claims to be the only place in Ginza that also splits its steamed eel to order — and a quarter of each fish is taken for shirayaki, because the freshness will show most in the fish served plain. Wild eel, the shop says up to two and a half times normal size and mostly from Lake Biwa, is aged about ten days before it is cooked. The supporting cast is specified to a degree that is unusual even in Ginza: Mikawa Sanshū mirin, haza-gake rice from Shiozawa in Uonuma, Rishiri kombu from Okui Kaiseidō, honkarebushi katsuobushi, and a room fitted out by an architect with the counter, chairs, cabinets, tableware and lighting all commissioned — reviewers describe it as a small museum, and there are Kitaōji Rosanjin pieces among the art. The kitchen is run by 高橋明宏 as fourth-generation 料理長 alongside a corporate 総料理長, 綾ゆうき, and 田中翔児 as executive chef. Guests choose Kansai-style crisp or Kantō-style soft grilling on arrival, and if the eel box at the end of a kaiseki defeats you the staff will box the whole thing or half of it to take away. Tabelog has selected it for the unagi Hyakumeiten in 2024 and 2026, and it carries a Michelin Guide Tokyo Selected Restaurant listing.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「革命-REVOLUTION」 in the eel trade without letting go of the tradition — an unagi shop built on the discipline of a ryōtei and a two-star kaiseki kitchen.
chef_bio.specialty: 割きたてうな重御膳 ¥8,800 — eel split to order, a quarter served as shirayaki on a separate plate; and the wild-eel 天然うな重御膳 at ¥19,800.

anecdotes.text: The shop dates its own line to 紫雲亭 around 1820, renamed 藤喜紫雲亭 around 1870 and 高橋屋 around 1890 — 'taken together, said to be two hundred years'.
It names its two influences openly: the Mitsui zaibatsu's ryōtei 松の茶屋, and Ginza Kojyu, the two-star kaiseki restaurant a few streets away — which happens to be another record in this same shard.
You are asked on arrival whether you want the eel grilled Kansai-style (crisp) or Kantō-style (soft) — a choice most Tokyo eel shops do not offer at all.
Live eel is brought to the table and explained before it is split, and the counter lets you watch the work; the staff are happy to be photographed doing it.
If the eel box at the end of a kaiseki course is more than you can finish, say so partway through and they will pack the whole thing or half of it to take home.
The takeaway うな重 bento is popular as a dressing-room lunch at the Kabuki-za next door.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: takahashiya-ginza.com is the shop's own site and carries the address 中央区銀座4-12-1 VORT銀座イーストⅡビル4F, phone 03-3547-0021, hours 11:30–16:00 and 17:00–22:00 with last orders, closing days (every Monday plus the second and third Tuesday), access from Higashi-Ginza exit A7, 14 seats, card acceptance, the average spend, and the descriptions of the wild eel, the ten-day ageing, the split-to-order practice and the three kaiseki courses. Tabelog's shop-managed listing adds the coordinates used here, the 103 m distance from Higashi-Ginza, the 14 August 2021 opening date, private rooms, the full current price list, the sourcing notes (Mikawa Isshiki eel, Sanshū mirin, Uonuma haza-gake rice, Okui Kaiseidō Rishiri kombu, honkarebushi), the named kitchen and management line-up including 四代目 料理長 高橋明宏, the 紫雲亭 → 藤喜紫雲亭 → 高橋屋 lineage, the sister shops at Sugito and Kawagoe, the Michelin Guide Tokyo Selected listing, and unagi Hyakumeiten selections for 2024 and 2026.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One binchōtan grill handles both tare-glazed kabayaki and plain shirayaki through the service; nothing separated is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house tare — described by the shop as an heirloom — is the standard soy, mirin and sugar glaze; wheat soy sauce, and not something the kitchen will substitute.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Live eel is split at the counter and the seasoning base is kombu and honkarebushi katsuobushi.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The listing explicitly invites the conversation: 「うなぎが苦手、うな重がダメな方、遠慮なく ご相談下さい」 and 「お時間 制限など御座いましたらお申し付け下さいませ」. That is a shop used to adjusting for individual guests, though it is about preference and pacing, not a stated allergen policy.
Reservations are taken (and walk-ins accepted), there is an English menu and English-speaking staff on the floor — so the request can actually be made and understood.

positives.text: A quarter of every eel is served 白焼き, grilled without tare, alongside freshly grated 生わさび rather than tubed wasabi paste — the most plausible starting point in this shard for a gluten-avoiding diner, if the kitchen confirms the salt and the soup.

cultural_comfort.note: Unusually accommodating for a Ginza counter of this price: reservations are taken but walk-ins are welcomed, there is an English menu, a photo menu and English-speaking staff, free Wi-Fi and power sockets, step-free access and wheelchair entry, and infants, pushchairs and children are all fine. Fourteen seats plus private rooms for eight or up to twenty; parties of ten to fourteen must take one of the two kaiseki courses. Cards accepted, no service charge, prices tax-inclusive. There is a dress code of sorts — no workwear and nothing extremely casual. Closed Mondays and the second and third Tuesday. If it is full, leave a mobile number and wait on the red chairs in the Kabuki-za tower next door.

name: 銀座 しのはら
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座2-8-17 ハビウル銀座2 B1
cuisine: A thirteen-seat basement counter doing one omakase kaiseki at ¥35,000, rewritten every month — a day's course might open with 七宝盛り, seven ingredients including abalone and sea urchin arranged as the seven treasures, and run through to a hassun built largely on Shiga produce; plates are called painting-like and the glassware includes old Baccarat, with service charge and tax on top
neighborhood: Ginza 2-chōme — 2 min from Ginza-itchōme Station on the Tokyo Metro Yūrakuchō line (154 m), 3 min from Ginza Station; the entrance is a small andon lantern at street level with the restaurant down the stairs
hours_raw: 月・水・金 17:00～23:00　火・木・土 12:00～15:00／17:00～23:00　日曜定休　※17時・20時30分の一斉スタート2回転、火・木・土のみ12時スタートの昼営業あり
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim exists, and a Japanese kaiseki course is wheat by default: the seasoning base is ordinary wheat soy sauce, there is normally a fried course, and 麩 turns up in soups. What this restaurant does have is the format that can absorb a request — thirteen seats, a single omakase, everything cooked to order in front of you, and a booking taken by phone up to three months out with a chef who rewrites the menu every month anyway. Nothing published shows a wheat-free line, so a celiac must raise it in Japanese at the time of booking and accept that the answer may be no.
vegan_detail: Nothing about vegan or vegetarian cooking is published. The course is built on seasonal seafood and katsuo dashi, so the default is emphatically not vegan; the only route is to ask when booking, months ahead, and there is no evidence anyone has been accommodated.

roles: 店主・料理長 (owner-chef)
chef_bio.origin: Shiga prefecture — the original しのはら was a Shiga restaurant, and Shiga produce still anchors the menu
chef_bio.background: Shinohara made his name in Shiga, where his restaurant しのはら drew serious eaters from across Japan. Then he did something unusual: he gave the whole thing up and started again in Tokyo, reopening as 銀座しのはら on 6 October 2016. He had trained at a series of well-known houses, 山玄茶 among them, and what he brought with him is a way of composing a plate that reviewers reach for the word 'painting' to describe. The room is deliberately understated — you find it by a small andon lantern at the building entrance and go down to the basement, into a plain, very clean space built around an L-shaped counter in white wood, with old Baccarat among the glassware. There is no menu: one omakase course, at ¥35,000, rewritten every month, which is the point for the regulars. A typical opening is the 七宝盛り, seven ingredients — abalone, sea urchin and others — presented as the seven Buddhist treasures; the hassun that closes the savoury run leans on Shiga. Thirteen seats, everything served in two synchronised sittings, and the booking line open for three hours a day. The results are on the record: The Tabelog Award has given it Gold every year from 2017 to 2026, it has been a Japanese-cuisine Hyakumeiten pick in 2021, 2023 and 2025, and the Michelin Guide Japan lists it at two stars for 2026.
chef_bio.philosophy: Give up the name you have already made and rebuild it. One course, no choices, rewritten monthly, on a counter small enough that the chef can see every plate land.
chef_bio.specialty: The monthly omakase — 七宝盛り to open, a Shiga-weighted hassun to close.

anecdotes.text: Shinohara abandoned an established reputation in Shiga to start over in Tokyo — Tabelog's own copy puts it as 「これまでの名声をすべて捨て、東京進出を決意」 — and reopened in Ginza on 6 October 2016.
There is no sign to speak of: a small andon lantern at the entrance, then stairs down to the basement.
The phone line for reservations is open only between 12:00 and 15:00, and the book runs about three months ahead.
Gold in The Tabelog Award every year from 2017 through 2026 — a ten-year run that very few restaurants in Japan hold.
No one under sixteen is seated.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog is the substantive source: the address 中央区銀座2-8-17 ハビウル銀座2 B1, the coordinates used here, the 154 m distance from Ginza-itchōme, phone 03-6263-0345, 完全予約制 with the 12:00–15:00 phone window and roughly three months' lead, the two-sitting service pattern with lunch only on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, Sunday closed, 13 counter seats, all non-smoking, cards accepted, service charge and tax additional, sixteen-and-over only, the 6 October 2016 opening date, and the single ¥35,000 omakase. Its editorial copy supplies Shinohara's Shiga background, the 山玄茶 training, the decision to leave for Tokyo, the 七宝盛り, the monthly menu change, the white-wood L-shaped counter and the old Baccarat. Tabelog also records Gold in The Tabelog Award for 2017–2026 and Japanese-cuisine Hyakumeiten for 2021, 2023 and 2025. The Michelin Guide's Japanese site lists 銀座 しのはら at two stars in the 2026 guide.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A single small kaiseki kitchen serving one course to thirteen people at a time. No dedicated wheat-free equipment is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No tamari or wheat-free seasoning is mentioned anywhere; assume ordinary wheat shōyu, and assume a fried course, as in any kaiseki of this length.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Seasonal seafood is the backbone of the course and bonito dashi the backbone of the seasoning.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Nothing is published about allergen handling. The booking is by telephone only, in a three-hour daily window, up to about three months ahead — which is the one and only opportunity to raise anything.

positives.text: A single omakase written fresh each month and cooked to order for thirteen people is, structurally, the kind of kitchen most able to work around a diner — if it agrees to in advance.

cultural_comfort.note: Among the harder doors in this shard. Reservations only, by telephone, in a 12:00–15:00 window, roughly three months ahead — no online booking channel is published by the restaurant, though the concierge platform OMAKASE appears in diners' accounts. Two synchronised sittings at 17:00 and 20:30, so you cannot drift in late. Thirteen seats at a counter in a basement with almost no signage, no private rooms, sixteen and over only, all non-smoking, cards accepted, service charge and tax on top of ¥35,000. There is no restaurant website and no English page; assume the evening runs in Japanese.

enrich_note: Confirmed and pinned at 中央区銀座2-8-17 ハビウル銀座2 B1, coordinates 35.672974/139.767871 from Tabelog; opened 6 October 2016 (Tabelog flags an earlier address, so any older pin is stale). The light record's Michelin two-star claim checks out — Michelin's Japanese guide lists 銀座 しのはら at two stars in the 2026 guide — and its truncated 'Tabelo…' was heading for the right place: Gold in The Tabelog Award every year 2017–2026. name: 銀座 小十
address_ja: 〒104-0061 東京都中央区銀座5丁目4-8 カリオカビル4F
cuisine: Two-star Japanese cuisine from Okuda Tōru, who cooks the season in three movements — 走り, 盛り, 名残, the arriving, the peak and the last of an ingredient — and takes his hands off the produce as far as he can; one chef's-choice course only, ¥33,000 at lunch and ¥41,800 at dinner (both tax included, plus 10% service), with the June bill of live young ayu and wild eel announced on the site each year
neighborhood: Ginza 5-chōme on Namiki-dōri, fourth floor of the Carioca building — 3 min from Ginza Station exit B6 (113 m), 10 min from JR Yūrakuchō central exit
hours_raw: 昼 12:00～12:30（最終入店）／夜 18:00～20:30（最終入店）　定休日：日曜日、祝日不定休、ゴールデンウィーク、夏季休暇　要予約
gf_detail: Nothing gluten-free is claimed and a kaiseki course of this length is wheat by default — wheat soy sauce as the seasoning base, a fried course in most menus, 麩 in soups. Against that, this is a reservation-only house with a single course, 22 seats including private rooms, a sommelier on staff and a chef who cooks to the day's market; the room can in principle build around a diner. It has not said it will. A celiac should raise it when booking, in Japanese, and treat a vague answer as a no.
vegan_detail: Tabelog files the restaurant under 野菜料理にこだわる — vegetables are taken seriously here, which matches the sweep's note — but taking vegetables seriously is not veganism: the course runs on seasonal fish and on katsuo dashi, and the house's own seasonal highlight is charcoal-grilled ayu and wild eel. No vegan or vegetarian course is published. Ask at booking; nothing is promised.

roles: 店主・料理長 (owner-chef), 銀座小十
オーナー, 銀座奥田 (2011) and OKUDA Paris (2013)
chef_bio.origin: Born 1969 in Shizuoka city, Shizuoka prefecture
chef_bio.background: Okuda spent about ten years learning Japanese cooking across Shizuoka, Kyoto and Tokushima before opening his own restaurant, 春夏秋冬 花見小路, in Shizuoka in November 1999. Ginza Kojyu followed in July 2003; he opened 銀座奥田 in August 2011, moved Kojyu to its present room on Namiki-dōri in Ginza 5-chōme in June 2012, and opened OKUDA in Paris in September 2013. His stated approach is to interrogate every ingredient and then interfere with it as little as possible — 「極力手を加えずに食材の滋味を引き出した繊細なひと皿」 — and to track the season in three stages rather than one: 走り, the first of a thing; 盛り, its peak; 名残, what is left of it as it goes. The room is built for that kind of attention: 22 seats over a counter, a sunken-hearth tatami space for six and two private rooms of four, quiet and generously spaced, all non-smoking, with a sommelier and a serious sake and wine list. There is one chef's-choice course at each service and nothing else. His own site barely updates, which the regulars treat as part of the character — but it reliably posts one thing each year as June approaches, the announcement of the house's live ayu and large wild eel, and diners plan around it. Okuda has been named 現代の名工, the government's Contemporary Master Craftsman award, and wrote about it on the shop's news page in terms of duty rather than triumph: Japanese cooking is the wisdom and technique held inside a tradition earlier generations built, and his job now is to pass the craft to the young cooks who will carry it. He has also published a book of the restaurant's soups and sashimi, 『銀座小十の椀と造り八十品』, through Seibundo Shinkosha. The Michelin Guide Japan lists Ginza Kojyu at two stars for 2026; The Tabelog Award gave it Bronze from 2017 to 2021 and it has been a Japanese-cuisine Hyakumeiten pick in 2021, 2023 and 2025.
chef_bio.philosophy: 走り・盛り・名残 — cook the arriving, the peak and the fading of each ingredient as three different dishes, and otherwise get out of the way.
chef_bio.specialty: The single chef's-choice course; in early summer, charcoal-grilled live young ayu and large wild eel, announced on the site each June.

anecdotes.text: The site is famously seldom updated, but every year as June approaches it posts the arrival of the live ayu and the big wild eel — regulars watch for it and book around it.
Okuda opened his first restaurant in Shizuoka in 1999, Kojyu in Ginza in 2003, and OKUDA in Paris in 2013 — the Ginza room moved to Namiki-dōri in June 2012.
On receiving 現代の名工 he wrote that his own technique mattered less than passing the craft on: 「今後も日本料理を受け継ぐ若い世代に素晴らしい技と魅力を伝え、未来永遠に繁栄されるものにしたい」.
He has published 『銀座小十の椀と造り八十品』, eighty of the restaurant's soups and sashimi, with Seibundo Shinkosha.
The unagi restaurant 銀座 四代目 高橋屋, a few streets away in Higashi-Ginza, names Ginza Kojyu — along with the Mitsui zaibatsu's ryōtei Matsu-no-Chaya — as one of the two houses its cooking is based on.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kojyu.jp is the operator's own bilingual site: the info page carries the address 中央区銀座5丁目4-8 カリオカビル4F, phone and fax, hours as last-entry times (lunch 12:00–12:30, dinner 18:00–20:30), the current prices of ¥33,000 lunch and ¥41,800 dinner including tax with 10% service on top and a note that the dinner price changes in October, the seat breakdown (8 counter, 6 sunken-hearth tatami, two private rooms of four), all non-smoking and reservation-only. The intro page gives Okuda's dated biography from his 1969 Shizuoka birth to the 2013 Paris opening. The news pages carry the 現代の名工 award and the book. Tabelog corroborates the address and coordinates, the 113 m distance from Ginza Station, phone 03-6215-9544, 完全予約制, 22 seats with private rooms, a 10% service charge, cards accepted, the 2003 opening and the move from 銀座8-5-25, and records Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2021 and Hyakumeiten 2021/2023/2025. Michelin's Japanese guide lists it at two stars for 2026.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One kaiseki kitchen serving a single course to 22 covers; no separated wheat-free preparation is claimed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No tamari or wheat-free seasoning is mentioned; assume ordinary wheat soy sauce throughout, and assume a fried course.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Seasonal fish and bonito dashi are the base of the cooking, and the house's own seasonal set piece is grilled ayu and wild eel.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Nothing about allergen handling is published in either the Japanese or the English pages. Booking is by phone or through the site's reservation page, which is the only channel to raise it.

positives.text: Reservation-only, one course, small covers, an English page and a sommelier — the structure that most easily absorbs a dietary request, if the request is made in advance.

cultural_comfort.note: Reservation-only, with last entry at 12:30 for lunch and 20:30 for dinner — arrive within that window or you are not seated. ¥33,000 lunch, ¥41,800 dinner, tax included, plus a 10% service charge; cards accepted, no e-money or QR. Twenty-two seats across an eight-seat counter, a sunken-hearth tatami room for six and two private rooms of four, all non-smoking. Closed Sundays, irregularly on public holidays, and for Golden Week and the summer break. The site carries a full English version including hours, prices and access, which makes this one of the more approachable two-star doors in Ginza — but a dietary request still needs to be made clearly at booking.

enrich_note: Confirmed and pinned at 中央区銀座5丁目4-8 カリオカビル4F, coordinates 35.671453/139.763021 from Tabelog; the shop's own access page gives the same address and the 3-minute walk from Ginza exit B6. Name written 銀座 小十 in kanji, which is how the restaurant, Tabelog and Michelin all write it — the light record's kana 「銀座こじゅ」 is the reading (Ginza Kojyu), and the operator's own domain is kojyu.jp, so this is a kana-vs-kanji gloss rather than a different business. Two live corrections to earlier data: the restaurant moved from 銀座8-5-25 to Namiki-dōri in June 2012, so any older pin is stale, and Tabelog's course prices (¥27,500 / ¥38,500) are out of date — the shop's own info page currently publishes ¥33,000 lunch and ¥41,800 dinner, plus 10% service, and warns that the dinner price changes again in October. Note also that the site is http-only; https://kojyu.jp does not resolve, which is worth knowing before anyone marks the link dead. Michelin's Japanese guide lists it at two stars for 2026.
